title: Merge Intervals
description: Sort by start, then sweep once: extend the last merged interval if the next overlaps; otherwise start a new one. O(n log n) sort + O(n) sweep.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I'm given a list of intervals like `[[1,3],[2,6],[8,10]]`, and I need to merge any that overlap and return the resulting list. So `[1,3]` and `[2,6]` would collapse into `[1,6]`."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Is the input sorted? (Almost always no — that's the first move.)
• Do touching intervals like `[1,4]` and `[4,5]` count as overlapping, or strictly disjoint? (Changes one operator: `<=` vs `<`.)
• Can I mutate the input array by sorting in place, or do I need to copy first?
• Are intervals always `[start, end]` with `start <= end`, or can they be reversed/empty?
• Return shape — array of arrays, sorted by start in the output?
sections.why: The touching-vs-strict question is the load-bearing clarification — it flips one comparator and silently changes the result on test cases like `[[1,4],[4,5]]`. Asking it up front signals you've already mapped the failure modes. The mutation question is the senior tell: sorting is the first move, and a real engineer asks before mutating someone else's array.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n^2) solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The brute force is to repeatedly scan the list for any pair that overlaps and merge them in place, repeating until no merges happen. Each pass is O(n^2) on the pair check, and you could need up to n passes in the worst case — so O(n^3) ugly. Even a cleaner version that does one O(n^2) all-pairs sweep into a union-find or set is still quadratic. Let me see if I can avoid the all-pairs check by imposing some order first."
sections.why: Two reasons to narrate this. (1) It anchors O(n log n) as a clean win — you're not just shaving a constant, you're collapsing a quadratic. (2) It plants the seed for sorting: the brute force is expensive because it has to check every pair to find overlaps. If you could guarantee that an interval only ever overlaps with the run immediately before it, you'd never need that pair check.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to sort-then-sweep?
sections.say:
"Two things scream sort-then-sweep here. (1) The problem is fundamentally about *order* — two intervals can only overlap if one starts before the other ends. (2) After sorting by start, the structure collapses to a single sweep: if `cur.start <= last.end` they overlap and I extend `last.end`; otherwise `cur` is the start of a new disjoint run, push it. The key invariant is that once I see a non-overlap, I *never* have to look back. Because the array is sorted by start, every future interval has a start ≥ `cur.start`, so it can't reach back across the gap into the previous run. That's what makes one pass sufficient.

The Math.max on the end is the one subtlety — `cur` might be fully contained in `last` (like `[1,4]` then `[2,3]`), in which case I must not shrink the run by overwriting `last.end` with the smaller value."
sections.why: Pattern-naming alone is a guess. The derivation — sorting buys you a no-look-back invariant, and the sweep maintains it in one pass — is what scores. The 'no need to look back after a non-overlap' insight is the load-bearing one; it's why this is O(n) sweep and not O(n^2), and naming it explicitly shows you understand *why* the algorithm is correct, not just that it works on the examples.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — a canonical mix with multiple merges, a touching-endpoints case that exercises the `<=`, and a contained case that exercises the Math.max.

examples.note: Canonical case — one merge, then two disjoint runs.
Touching endpoints — exercises the `<=` decision; `<` would split these wrongly.
examples.trace:
sort → [[1,4],[4,5]] (already sorted)
seed res = [[1,4]]
i=1 cur=[4,5], last=[1,4] → 4 <= 4 → OVERLAP (touching counts). last[1] = max(4,5) = 5 → res=[[1,5]]
return [[1,5]]

examples.note: Contained case — exercises the Math.max; without it last.end would shrink from 4 to 3.
examples.trace:
sort → [[1,4],[2,3]] (already sorted by start)
seed res = [[1,4]]
i=1 cur=[2,3], last=[1,4] → 2 <= 4 → OVERLAP. last[1] = max(4,3) = 4 (NOT 3) → res=[[1,4]]
return [[1,4]]

sections.why: Two specific bugs the trace exposes. (1) On `[[1,4],[2,3]]`, a naive `last[1] = cur[1]` would corrupt the run to `[1,3]` — the Math.max is what keeps the run honest when `cur` is fully contained. (2) On `[[1,4],[4,5]]`, the `<=` vs `<` choice flips the entire output; tracing forces you to commit to one and confirm against the spec before writing the loop.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Empty input `[]` → guard up front, return `[]`. The seed `res = [intervals[0]]` would crash without this.
• Single interval `[[1,2]]` → seed sets `res = [[1,2]]`, loop runs zero times, returns `[[1,2]]`. ✓
• All identical `[[1,5],[1,5],[1,5]]` → each subsequent one overlaps and Math.max keeps last.end at 5. Returns `[[1,5]]`.
• Fully nested `[[1,10],[2,3],[4,5]]` → after sort, every later interval is contained in the first; Math.max keeps the run at `[1,10]`.
• Already disjoint and sorted `[[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]]` → never overlaps, every iteration pushes; returns the input.
• Reverse-sorted input `[[15,18],[8,10],[1,6]]` → the sort fixes it; the sweep never sees the original order.
• Negative coordinates, zero-width intervals like `[[3,3]]` — the comparators all still work; no special case needed."
sections.why: The empty-input guard is the cheap obvious one but it's also the most common skipped check — `res = [intervals[0]]` crashes silently as `res = [undefined]` and the loop never errors, just returns garbage. Naming the fully-nested case explicitly is the dedup callout that proves the Math.max is doing real work, not decoration.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n log n), dominated entirely by the sort. The sweep itself is O(n) — one pass, constant work per element. Space is O(n) for the result array (in the worst case, no merges happen and `res` ends up the same size as `intervals`). The sort is in-place so it contributes O(log n) stack overhead for V8's quicksort, which I'd mention but it's not the bottleneck.

If you wanted to handle a stream of intervals arriving one at a time instead of a batch, you'd swap this for a sorted-set structure keyed by start, find the insertion point with binary search, and merge against neighbors — O(log n) per insert. That's the Insert Interval / Calendar Booking variant."
sections.why: The 'sort dominates' answer is the correct framing — most candidates state O(n log n) without naming *which step* drives it, which leaves them stuck when the interviewer asks 'what if the input came in pre-sorted?'. The streaming extension proves you see the family of problems: Insert Interval, My Calendar I/II, Range Module are all the same shape with different freshness assumptions.

reference.approach: Sort by start, then linear sweep
notes: Sort by START. After sorting, compare a candidate only against the LAST merged interval.
Touching intervals overlap with `<=`; use `<` if the problem says strictly disjoint.
Take Math.max of ends — the next interval may be fully contained; you must not shrink the run.
reference.crux: Sort by start, then sweep comparing each interval to ONLY the last merged one: overlap (start <= last.end) extends it via Math.max, otherwise it begins a new run. No look-back needed.
cruxDistractors: Repeatedly scan for any overlapping pair and merge them, looping until no merges remain — correct but O(n^2) or worse.
Sort by END instead of start, then sweep and merge each interval into the previous one.
On overlap, set last.end = cur.end directly instead of Math.max — which shrinks the run when cur is fully contained.

alternates.label: Union-Find (DSU) on overlapping intervals
alternates.when: Reach for this when the problem morphs into 'add an interval and re-merge' (Insert Interval, dynamic calendar) or when intervals arrive as a stream and you need to keep merging incrementally without re-sorting. Sort+sweep is one-shot — DSU gives you a structure that absorbs new overlaps in near-constant amortized time per union.
notes: Two intervals [a0,a1] and [b0,b1] overlap iff a0 <= b1 AND b0 <= a1 — the classic 'one starts before the other ends, both ways' test.
Path compression in `find` keeps the amortized cost per union near-constant; the O(n²) bound is from the pairwise overlap scan, not the DSU itself.
DSU shines on the Insert Interval / dynamic-calendar followup: incoming intervals just `union` with whatever they overlap, no re-sort needed.

questions.q: Why sort by start before merging?
options: So the output is automatically returned in sorted order, satisfying the spec without a final sort pass
Lets us compare each interval to only the last merged one — one pass suffices
Sorting compacts the array in memory, eliminating cache misses on the sweep
So binary search can locate the merge target in O(log n) instead of O(n)
questions.explain: With starts ascending, anything that overlaps must overlap the most recently merged run, so `res[res.length - 1]` is the only interval to compare against and one pass suffices.

options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n + k log k) where k = number of merged runs
questions.explain: `intervals.sort(...)` dominates at O(n log n); the merge sweep itself is a single O(n) pass.

questions.q: When merging, why use Math.max(last[1], cur[1])?
options: Because `last[1]` is read from a shared reference and could mutate during the iteration; Math.max snapshots it
cur may end before last — taking the max prevents shrinking the run
Math.max is required to extend the array correctly because JS array indexing rounds towards zero
Because sorting only orders starts, not ends, so `cur[1]` might be larger and Math.max picks it
questions.explain: Sorting orders starts only, so `cur` can sit entirely inside `last` — a plain `last[1] = cur[1]` would then SHRINK the run. The max is there for the cur-ends-earlier case, not the cur-ends-later one.

questions.q: Should touching intervals like [1,4] and [4,5] merge?
options: Always — they share an endpoint
Never — disjoint endpoints means disjoint intervals
Only when the problem says so; check `<=` vs `<`
Only when sorting by end (not start) — because end-sort places them adjacent
questions.explain: The canonical's `cur[0] <= last[1]` merges `[1,4]` with `[4,5]` into `[1,5]`; switching to `<` keeps them apart — the operator IS the spec decision, not a fixed rule.

questions.q: Which key do you sort by, and why that one?
options: By end — so the longest intervals come first
By start — once starts are ascending, any overlap must touch the most recently merged interval, so one pass suffices
By interval width
Either start or end works the same
questions.explain: Sorting by start guarantees later intervals can only overlap the last merged run (their start is >= everything before), which is what collapses the problem to a single sweep.

questions.q: After sorting by start, the overlap test for the current interval vs the last merged one is:
options: cur.start <= last.end
cur.end <= last.start
cur.start >= last.end
cur.end >= last.end
questions.explain: Since starts are sorted, cur.start is already >= last.start; they overlap exactly when cur begins at or before last ends, i.e. cur.start <= last.end.

questions.q: Why is one forward pass enough — never looking back at earlier merged intervals?
options: Because the array is short
Sorted starts mean every future interval starts at or after the current one, so it can never reach back across a gap into an older run
Because intervals never overlap
Because Math.max handles it
questions.explain: Ascending starts give a no-look-back invariant: once a gap closes a run, no later interval can start before that gap, so earlier runs are final — that is why the sweep is O(n).

questions.q: What guards against crashing on an empty input `[]`?
options: The sort call
An up-front `if (intervals.length === 0) return []` — otherwise `res = [intervals[0]]` seeds with undefined
Math.max
Nothing is needed
questions.explain: Without the guard, seeding `res = [intervals[0]]` on an empty array yields `[undefined]` and silently returns garbage; the length check is the cheap fix.

blanks.hint: do not shrink the run if cur ends earlier

L3.prompt: Implement `merge(intervals)` that returns merged intervals (touching = overlap). Log `JSON.stringify(merge([[1,4],[4,5]]))`.
hints: Sort by start, then sweep once.
Use Math.max(last[1], cur[1]) — cur could be fully inside last.
